title: Two-hundred-variant bit-cell zoo on every shuttle run
idea: MAGNIFY variants and MINIFY cost per experiment: tile 200 bit-cell variants (gain cells, varactor caps, bootstrapped switches, leakage latches) with on-die retention/endurance BIST on each $10-20k MPW shuttle, publish an open retention-tail database and license the winners.
why: Cuts cell-discovery cycles from years to quarters and feeds U.S. fabs with characterized cells (facts 3, 4).
note: Cheap MPW characterization; incremental discovery value.

title: Thousand-composition sputter library hunts for k-over-100 dielectrics
idea: MAGNIFY experiment throughput ~1000x: co-sputter three targets with deliberate thickness gradients onto one 150-mm wafer pre-patterned with 1,000 MIM test capacitors, then auto-probe k, leakage at 1 V and breakdown overnight, screening ternary oxide spaces such as Ti-Zr-La-O weekly.
why: A fast, cheap route to k >= 70 at <= 1e-7 A/cm2 (fact 1) without big-fab capital.
note: Composition-spread high-k searches date to Bell Labs 1998; cheap and fast but well-trodden.

title: Cloud DFT screen for a k-70 dielectric that ALD can grow
idea: Worsen: keep the k ~40 ZrO2 stack forever. Flip: spend ~$300k of cloud compute on a high-throughput DFT and phonon screen of rutile and alloyed oxides (Ti-Ge-Sn-O, Hf-Ti-O) for k >= 70 with band gap >= 4 eV and ALD growth below 450 C, then test the top five in a university ALD within 24 months.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): k 70 lets AR fall from 75:1 to ~45:1, a cheap route to a step change.
note: High-throughput DFT dielectric databases exist; ALD realizability of predicted phases is the doubt.

title: Po: the worst transistor is the best — cryo poly-Si 3D stack
idea: Po: the worst transistor is the best. Extracted: build 128-tier 1T1C stacks with cheap, leaky low-temperature poly-Si TFT access devices using a NAND-like single-hole etch and no EUV, then run the module at ~150 K where trap-assisted leakage drops by orders of magnitude, turning unusable cells into seconds-retention DRAM.
why: Accepting a cryocooler unlocks the cheapest 3D flow (near NAND cost, ~100x below DRAM contract) and also lowers wire resistance. Trade-offs: cooling power and cold packaging.
note: Cryo rescues leaky NAND-style 3D 1T1C; doubt: field-enhanced trap tunneling and GIDL do not freeze out, plus cooling overhead.

title: Logic-die decoupling capacitors double as on-demand scratch memory
idea: Invert 'storage elements must be dedicated memory cells' -> reuse the capacitors already on every logic die. An accelerator's deep-trench/MIM decap is split into ~50 fF segments with access switches, so idle decap banks act as eDRAM-like scratch when the supply-noise budget allows and revert to decoupling during load surges.
why: ~15% of an 800 mm^2 die at ~500 nF/mm^2 is ~1e9 storable bits (~100+ MB) of near-compute memory with ~zero added wafer area, cutting data-movement energy (fact 5) and DRAM demand.

title: Endohedral ion-in-cage dipole: one molecule, one bit
idea: Scarcity rule: the bit gets one molecule of space. A metal ion inside an elongated fullerene or nitride-cluster cage (Li+@C70-type) sits in one of two off-center wells, a gate field flips it, and the dipole shifts the threshold of an underlying 2D transistor. No bond breaks, and the cage is chosen for a ~0.8 eV barrier giving ms-s retention.
why: Self-assembled monolayer density near 1 nm2 per bit bypasses the litho wall (fact 4) with attojoule writes and unbounded cycling; barrier engineering and single-molecule readout are speculative.
note: ~1 nm2 bits would be huge, but sensing a single molecule's dipole via a transistor at that pitch needs a miracle.

title: Thermally drawn fiber preforms yield coaxial capacitor bundles
idea: Adapt optical-fiber drawing: build a macroscopic preform of metal/glass/metal coaxial rods, draw it ~1000x down to 30 nm features over km lengths, slice it into thin wafers of parallel coaxial capacitors, and hybrid-bond them onto access-transistor wafers.
why: Facts 1 and 4: any aspect ratio for the price of drawing glass, with no HAR etch or EUV in the capacitor; registration to transistors is the main risk.
note: Capacitor length becomes slice thickness, decoupling AR from etch; registration and 30 nm draw breakup are doubts.

title: Leakage decay as built-in recency weighting for analog KV caches
idea: Invert 'charge decay is a failure that refresh must undo' -> make decay part of the math. KV-cache and state-space values are stored as un-refreshed analog charge whose leakage time constant is programmed per bank by body bias, so stored magnitude decays exponentially with token age, implementing the recency weighting (decay gates, ALiBi-like bias) models already learn.
why: Eliminates refresh for the largest AI memory consumer (fact 3) and stores 4-6 analog bits per cell, multiplying effective capacity 4-6x for inference KV caches.

title: Apollo core-rope ROM reborn as via-coupled multi-layer weight store
idea: Apollo's rope memory encoded bits as whether a sense wire threaded a core. Encode frozen AI weights as presence or absence of via stubs coupling word lines to sense lines across 8 metal-layer pairs of an existing 40-nm logic process (one custom via mask per layer); pulsing a word line induces charge only on sense lines with a stub, so there is no DC sneak path.
why: Frees DRAM/HBM now spent on immutable weights; no refresh, no capacitor; 8 planes x 4F2 at 40 nm is ~800 nm2 per bit, about DRAM's 864 nm2, at far lower capex and no EUV.
note: Hardwired-weight inference (via ROM) exists; inflexible to model updates.

title: Via-programmed ROM for frozen model weights frees DRAM
idea: Combine mask-ROM economics with AI inference: weights frozen for a product's life are encoded in one via layer (1-2F2 per bit, multi-level via resistance for 2 bits) on a die whose other masks are shared, so only the via mask changes per model, written by e-beam or DUV. The weights never need refresh, never wear out, and stop occupying HBM.
why: Weights are a large share of inference memory; moving them to refresh-free ROM at ~1/5 the cost per bit releases that DRAM supply.
note: Hardwired-model silicon already pursued (e.g., Taalas); model churn limits benefit.

title: Charge-gated Mott channel amplifies a few hundred stored electrons
idea: Effect walk: filling-controlled Mott transition. The storage node gates a 3-nm channel of a correlated oxide (strained NdNiO3 or electron-doped Sr2IrO4) poised at its metal-insulator boundary, so a few hundred stored electrons (~0.1-0.3 e per unit cell under a 100 nm2 gate) swing channel resistance ~100x for a gain read.
why: Cuts required storage charge ~100x (5 fF to ~0.03-0.05 fF), removing the high-AR capacitor (fact 1) and shrinking the cell toward 4F2; risks are retaining so few electrons against the leakage tail and Mott-channel variability.
note: Big charge cut if it works, but gating ~1e14 cm-2 electrostatically needs near-breakdown fields; 3 nm Mott-oxide variability.

title: Long-channel thick-oxide gain cell in open-source 130 nm
idea: MAGNIFY channel length ~10x and oxide thickness ~3x on the write device: a 3T gain cell in the open SKY130/GF180 PDKs uses the 5 V thick-oxide transistor as write switch (aA subthreshold leakage) and stores on the read transistor's gate; free or cheap shuttles allow monthly iterations.
why: Retention ~1-10 s vs 64 ms (fact 3) in U.S.-fabbed nodes with near-zero capital; niche embedded DRAM for chiplets.
note: Gain-cell eDRAM in open PDKs already explored; niche.
